questions.q: Define the term ‘developmental milestone’ in the context of early childhood (2–6 years) and give one example each from the physical, cognitive, and social domains.
questions.a: A developmental milestone is an observable skill or behaviour that most children achieve within a typical age range, used to track progress across domains. Example: Physical – hopping on one foot (age 4–5); Cognitive – using sentences of 4–5 words (age 4); Social – engaging in cooperative play with peers (age 4–5). A wrong answer that lists only one domain or gives infant milestones (e.g., rolling over) shows the student cannot differentiate early childhood from infancy or misses the multi‑domain nature of development.

questions.q: A 3‑year‑old child builds a tower of 6 blocks, names colours correctly, but does not share toys and says “Mine!” when another child approaches. Using Piaget’s and Erikson’s frameworks, explain why this behaviour is developmentally typical.
questions.a: Piaget’s preoperational stage (2–7 years) includes symbolic play (building towers) and egocentrism (difficulty seeing others’ perspectives), so not sharing is normal. Erikson’s stage “initiative vs. guilt” (3–6 years) involves asserting control; saying “Mine!” reflects emerging initiative and possession sense. A wrong answer that labels the child as “selfish” or “delayed” reveals a misunderstanding of egocentrism as a cognitive limitation rather than a moral flaw, and confusion between psychosocial initiative and behavioural problems.

questions.q: Design a simple 5‑item observation checklist for a preschool teacher to monitor physical, cognitive, and social milestones of 4‑year‑olds during free play. Each item must be observable, domain‑specific, and age‑appropriate.
questions.a: Checklist: (1) Physical – hops on one foot for 2 seconds; (2) Physical – copies a cross (+) with pencil; (3) Cognitive – tells a short story using 4–5 word sentences; (4) Cognitive – matches 4 colours correctly; (5) Social – engages in cooperative play with 1–2 peers for 5 minutes. A wrong answer that includes items like “writes name” (too advanced) or “shares willingly always” (ignores egocentrism) shows inability to select age‑appropriate, observable indicators.

questions.q: Compare the physical growth patterns of early childhood (2–6 years) with infancy (0–2 years) in terms of rate, body proportions, and brain development. Explain how these differences affect motor skill acquisition.
questions.a: Infancy: rapid growth (weight triples, height increases 50%), head large relative to body, brain reaches 75% adult weight by age 2. Early childhood: slower, steady growth (2–3 kg/year, 5–7 cm/year), legs lengthen, trunk slims, brain reaches 90% adult weight by age 6 with synaptic pruning. Motor skills shift from reflexive/large‑muscle (rolling, sitting) to refined gross (hopping, skipping) and fine (drawing, buttoning) due to myelination and cerebellar maturation. A wrong answer that claims growth rate stays high or that brain growth is complete by age 2 indicates confusion between infancy and early childhood trajectories.

questions.q: Critique the statement: “If a 5‑year‑old cannot read simple words, they are cognitively delayed.” Use concepts of developmental appropriateness, domain interplay, and individual variation.
questions.a: Reading simple words is not a universal milestone for age 5; NCERT places emergent literacy (recognizing letters, pretend reading) at 5–6 years, with formal reading emerging later. Cognitive delay must be assessed across multiple domains (language, memory, problem‑solving), not a single skill. Individual variation in exposure to print, home language, and teaching methods affects timing. A wrong answer that agrees with the statement shows a lack of understanding of age‑appropriate expectations and the multi‑factorial nature of literacy development.

questions.q: Create a one‑page parent handout (outline only) titled “What to Expect at Ages 2–6” that integrates physical, cognitive, and social milestones into three monthly age bands (2–3, 3–4, 4–5, 5–6 years). Include one practical tip per band for supporting development.
questions.a: Outline: Band 1 (2–3 yrs): Physical – runs, kicks ball; Cognitive – 2‑word sentences, symbolic play; Social – parallel play, “no” phase. Tip: Provide safe climbing space. Band 2 (3–4 yrs): Physical – pedals tricycle, copies circle; Cognitive – 3–4 word sentences, asks “why”; Social – initiates play, shares with prompts. Tip: Read picture books daily. Band 3 (4–5 yrs): Physical – hops, draws person with 3 parts; Cognitive – tells story, counts 5 objects; Social – cooperative play, follows simple rules. Tip: Play board games with turns. Band 4 (5–6 yrs): Physical – skips, copies triangle; Cognitive – recognizes letters, writes name; Social – negotiates, shows empathy. Tip: Encourage storytelling. A poor answer that lists only one domain per band or gives infant skills reveals inability to synthesize cross‑domain progression.
